item.title: The Browser's Main Thread Is Expensive (25 minute read)
item.description: The browser's main thread runs JavaScript, handles input, and performs most of the rendering pipeline, leaving roughly 10ms of usable time per frame on a 60Hz display. Any task over 50ms risks visible jank. This guide shows how to split work around frame budgets, batch noisy events with debounce or throttle, prioritize and defer tasks, move animation to the compositor, use workers for atomic heavy work, and eliminate unnecessary computation.

item.title: Running LLMs in the Browser with Three.js (17 minute read)

This post walks through token generation, KV caches, architecture differences, and the optimizations that mattered: one command submission raised TinyStories decoding from about 120 to 566 tokens per second.

item.title: How Turbopack chunks your JavaScript (8 minute read)
item.description: Turbopack's chunker balances fewer requests against over-shipping code by merging small chunks only within route chunk groups and weighting single-page versus multi-page sessions. On nextjs.org, its defaults reduced 96 requests to 38 while slightly cutting downloaded JavaScript from 561.6 KiB to 554.8 KiB. Next.js 16.3 adds experimental cache-aware component chunks, analytics-informed route priorities and clusters, CommonJS tree shaking, a shared runtime, and a lighter default runtime.

item.title: The asteroid currently hitting frontend web development (10 minute read)

It's built on a weighted 0-100 score over a rolling 50-action window feeding four tiers (T1 Probation → T4 Autonomous) that promote slowly with hysteresis but demote immediately.

item.title: Small Models Have Arrived (4 minute read)
item.description: Recent advancements in AI models like gpt-5.6-luna and GLM 5.3 show that smaller, faster models are becoming increasingly capable and cost-effective, especially for tasks that require responsiveness rather than extreme intelligence. As the demand for "fast/cheap/good-enough" AI solutions rises, there is potential for faster, cheaper development in business applications.

item.title: Growing Lazyweb to 50k+ Agents (6 minute read)
item.description: Lazyweb successfully grew to over 50,000 agents without any marketing spend, experimenting with various distribution channels and growth tactics. A range of strategies were implemented, from reducing friction for users to using storytelling and engaging with communities.

item.title: BrowserSkill (GitHub Repo)

item.description: The Context Engineering Kit is a development toolkit designed to improve the quality and efficiency of AI-generated code through techniques like specification-driven development, subagent-driven workflows, and various plugins that optimize coding practices and improve result reliability.

item.title: Making Your Data Ready for Agentic AI (42 minute read)
item.description: To prepare data for autonomous AI agents, organizations must transition from traditional data systems designed for human analysts to structures that make sure data is trusted, contextualized, and actionable, with layers such as data contracts, context layers, and controlled access. This shift requires a focus on data governance, traceability, and the integration of well-defined semantic models to make sure agents can operate confidently and correctly.

item.title: Why AI coding agents need context graphs (10 minute read)
item.description: AI coding agents fail in real codebases due to missing scattered team context, so the fix is an externally queryable context graph of typed entities and relationships. The API layer is a graph that teams already have, and if they are published with ownership metadata and MCP access, agents can perform better.

item.title: The best workflow engine is a programming language (11 minute read)
item.description: Using a programming language as a workflow engine simplifies the process of orchestrating long-running, stateful logic on unreliable infrastructure, allowing developers to write workflows in a more intuitive manner. item.title: DuckDB and the changing physics of analytics (18 minute read)
item.description: The rise of analytics engines like DuckDB shows a shift in data processing, driven by advancements in hardware that allow for efficient single-host operations rather than relying solely on distributed systems. As data processing demands have evolved, DuckDB enables developers to perform complex analytics directly within their applications, blurring the lines between data processing and application development. This is part of the reason AWS acquired DuckLabs.

item.title: VMs won't contain cyber-capable agents (9 minute read)
item.description: Recent testing revealed that advanced AI agents can quickly escape VMs by exploiting known and unknown vulnerabilities in host systems, leading to concerns about the adequacy of traditional virtualization for containment. To improve cybersecurity, it's necessary to adopt virtualization technologies designed with minimal attack surfaces and prioritize rapid software updates.

item.title: The process of migrating from Sass to native CSS (4 minute read)
item.description: The migration from Sass to native CSS is becoming increasingly viable as native CSS has incorporated many features previously exclusive to Sass, such as variables and functions. Replacing Sass may streamline projects by reducing complexity, improving build times, and eliminating unnecessary dependencies, and migration is now easier with AI.

item.title: The choices we make about AI now are critical (30 minute read)
item.description: The advent of AI presents both huge opportunities and monumental risks, potentially revolutionizing industries while simultaneously threatening job stability and economic equity. To make sure the benefits of this technology are shared broadly, a coordinated global response involving policymakers, industry leaders, and communities is necessary to address the challenges it poses.

item.title: WebSockets vs. SSE should be about ordering and correctness (6 minute read)
item.description: The real WebSockets-vs-SSE question isn't about latency or payload but ordering and correctness. Data split across two streams can race (a tag add and remove arriving out of order leaves the UI permanently stale). WebSockets are bidirectional, so reads and writes share one connection and the server can recompute and send the correct result regardless of order.

item.description: Progress in software development has accelerated due to advancements that allow single developers to achieve productivity levels comparable to larger teams by effectively using AI models within a structured "harness."
